package_info.why_malicious: The analyzed threats involve the injection of malicious JavaScript into a legitimate e-commerce payment page to steal sensitive customer data (web skimming), and the distribution of a destructive wiper malware disguised as a PDF attachment in phishing emails. Both attacks result in severe compromise of user data and/or permanent data loss, representing clear, high-impact malicious activity.

execution_context.file_location: Garmin South African shopping site (injected JavaScript on payment page)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a user interacts with the checkout/payment form, the code attaches a submit event listener, collects sensitive payment and personal data from form fields, and sends this data via HTTPS POST to a hardcoded attacker-controlled domain, resulting in exfiltration of customer information.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code intercepts form submissions on a payment page, collects sensitive data (credit card, address, phone, email), and exfiltrates it to an untrusted external domain, which is a classic web skimming tactic.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate e-commerce scripts should only transmit payment data to authorized payment processors or trusted services, never to unknown or hardcoded external domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate scripts may send form data to payment gateways or fraud detection services, but only to vetted, documented endpoints and never to arbitrary or hardcoded domains.
key_indicators: JavaScript code that hooks into payment form submission events
Collection of sensitive fields (credit card, address, phone, email) from the DOM
Network requests (fetch/POST) to hardcoded, untrusted external domains
Presence of injected or unauthorized JavaScript on sensitive pages

execution_context.file_location: Email attachment (PDF file with embedded executable payload)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when the user opens the disguised PDF attachment, the embedded executable iterates over user files, overwrites each file with random data, and then displays a fake ransomware message, resulting in irreversible data destruction and attempted extortion.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The executable masquerades as a PDF, and upon execution, it irreversibly overwrites all user files with random data, then displays a ransom note. This is destructive and deceptive, with no legitimate justification.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A PDF attachment, especially in a job application context, should never execute code or modify user files. Executable content in a document is a clear violation of user trust and system security.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate scenario where a PDF or job application attachment would overwrite user files or display a ransom note. Such behavior is exclusive to malware.
key_indicators: Executable file disguised with a .pdf or double extension in email attachments
Mass file overwrite operations targeting user data
Display of a ransom note after destructive actions
Absence of actual encryption—files are destroyed, not recoverable

attack_chain.action: Malicious JavaScript is injected into the shopping site’s payment page.
attack_chain.leads_to: Collection of payment and personal data from customers.

attack_chain.action: JavaScript code captures form data and sends it to an attacker-controlled server.
Victim receives a spam email with a PDF attachment that is actually an executable.
attack_chain.leads_to: User opens the attachment, triggering the payload.

attack_chain.action: Executable overwrites all user files with garbage and displays a fake ransom note.
attack_chain.leads_to: Permanent data loss and attempted extortion.

behavioral_signatures: JavaScript code that attaches event listeners to payment or checkout forms and exfiltrates form data to untrusted domains
Client-side scripts making network requests (e.g., fetch/POST) to hardcoded or unrecognized external endpoints
Email attachments with double extensions (e.g., .pdf.exe) or PE executables masquerading as documents
Processes that perform mass file overwrite operations followed by the display of a ransom note or message
file_indicators: Unexpected or unauthorized JavaScript modifications on payment/checkout pages
User files replaced with random or unreadable content after opening an attachment
Presence of ransom note files or pop-up messages after file destruction
network_indicators: Outbound HTTPS POST requests from client-side scripts to domains not associated with the legitimate business (e.g., hardcoded exfiltration endpoints)
Connections to known malicious exfiltration domains or IP addresses as identified in threat intelligence feeds
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor sensitive web pages for unauthorized JavaScript changes, especially scripts that access form fields and send data to unknown or hardcoded domains. Implement email gateway filtering to flag and quarantine attachments with double extensions or executable content disguised as documents. Deploy endpoint monitoring to detect processes that perform mass file overwrite operations and display ransom notes. Correlate network logs for suspicious outbound connections from client-side scripts to untrusted domains.
